newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trade gap rises 17.0 percent in May.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trade gap rises 17.0 percent in May.

text.p: The U.S. trade deficit in May soared by 17.0 percent to $10.23 billion as imports rose for the seventh straight month to a record high, the Commerce Department said on Friday.

The department said May exports fell 0.8 percent to $77.2 billion, reflecting a drop in exports of capital goods, such as telecommunications equipment. Imports continued their steady upward march, rising by a modest 1.0 percent in May to $87.5 billion, led by demand for capital goods, primarily civilian aircraft and automobiles, the department said.

The resulting May trade deficit exceeded the expectations of Wall Street analysts, who were looking for a $9.18 billion May trade gap. The April trade gap was revised upward to $8.75 billion from the $8.36 billion originally reported.
The U.S. trade deficit with China widened by 9.1 percent in May to $3.76 billion from $3.45 billion in April. The gap was the highest since since the October 1996 deficit of $4.9 billion.
The U.S. trade deficit with China surpassed that of Japan, only the third time that has happened, the department noted.
The politically sensitive deficit with Japan was the lowest since last June. The gap shrank by 25 percent to $3.63 billion from $4.84 billion in April.

In June numbers released Thursday, Japan said its bilateral trade surplus grew for the third consecutive month. Japanese officials stressed that the recent rise in the trade surplus was due to the special factor of a consumption tax hike.

The May trade data showed the U.S. trade gaps with Canada and Mexico widening, with the news coming just days after the Clinton administration hailed the benefits of the North American Free Trade Agreement.
The pact, which went into effect at the beginning of 1994, links the United States, Canada and Mexico in a trading bloc.

The U.S. trade deficit with Mexico swelled by 21.7 percent to a record $1.7 billion from $1.4 billion in April. In trade with Canada, the deficit more than doubled, rising 104.1 percent to $1.74 billion in May.
Imports from Canada of $14.5 billion in May were the highest on record with any country, the department said.
The United States had a deficit with Western Europe of $1.29 billion after recording a $486 million deficit in April.

Analysts said ahead of the report that it would not be surprising if imports rose in view of the high levels of consumer confidence and a booming domestic economy. Analysts have noted that a stronger dollar has reduced the cost of non-petroleum imports.
Foreign sales of civilian aircraft rose to $2.61 billion from $2.40 billion in April.
The merchandise trade gap rose 9.8 percent in May to $17.0 billion, while the services surplus rose 0.5 percent to $6.81 billion, the department said.
The cost of imported crude oil rose in May to $4.6 billion as the price per barrel dropped to $17 from $17.17 in April and $18.72 in March.
